name: Fermented rice water (sake lees)

lead: Sake lees (sake kasu) is the white pressed residue left after sake is drawn from fermented rice mash, long used in Japanese cooking. In skincare it goes into face masks, creams and bath powder for a brighter, moisturized, more even complexion, and users report a glow after use.

Freeze-dried kasu is reported to contain an extract that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme involved in pigment production, and the masks also carry antioxidants. No clinical trials in the sources reviewed tested it for appearance.

paras: It is used as a mask or cream, or dissolved in a bath, typically on a regular routine and alongside sunscreen. Benefits are described as brightening and softness over repeated use.
Kasu contains alcohol (around 8 percent), and sunscreen is advised for users of the masks. No safety trials in skincare were found.

angle.text: Sake lees is used in J-beauty masks, creams and bath powders for a brighter, moisturized complexion. Users report a glow after use, and laboratory work found it contains a tyrosinase-inhibiting extract, which acts on the enzyme involved in pigment production.

lead: Sake lees, known in Japanese as sake kasu, is the white paste left after fermented rice mash is pressed to make sake. It is used in Japanese cooking and in skin care, in face masks, bath powders and creams, and in homemade masks mixed with ingredients such as citrus juice, honey, rice water or aloe vera. People use it to aim for brighter, softer and more even-looking skin [1].

Users quoted on Wikipedia report softer, more moisturised skin, less redness from acne, fainter age spots and tighter pores. Proponents credit antioxidants and say it may support collagen, and a folktale of a brewery worker with smooth hands is used in marketing [1]. A laboratory finding that an extract of freeze-dried sake kasu inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme involved in pigment production, is the basis for describing it as a possible brightening or anti-browning ingredient [1].

Fermented rice water, a related home preparation, is discussed on hair-care forums, and news outlets have covered rice-water toners for hair growth [2][3][4]. Rice water has been used for centuries by women in China, Japan and Southeast Asia, and Wikipedia reports that Heian-period Japanese women reportedly kept very long hair healthy by soaking it in rice water [2].

No controlled human trial of topical sake lees or fermented rice water for skin or hair appearance has been published; research on sake lees concerns it as a food and in laboratory and animal models [5][6][7].

paras: During sake brewing, koji mold (Aspergillus oryzae) breaks rice starch into sugar and yeast converts the sugar to alcohol; the mash is pressed to extract sake, leaving the kasu [1]. Typical kasu contains about 8% alcohol, protein, carbohydrates, fat, B vitamins, fibre, peptides and amino acids, and is part of Japan's no-waste food culture; one brewer estimated about 250 litres of kasu for every 700 litres of sake, and hot growing seasons yield more kasu and milder sake [1].

Kasu is used in cooking as a marinade for fish, vegetables and meat, adding umami, and in pickling (kasuzuke), soups (kasujiru), crackers, breads and sweets [1]. Amazake is a sweet Japanese rice drink in two versions, one made with koji and one made with sake kasu plus sugar. Amazake dates to the Kofun period and is widely regarded in Japan as a hangover drink, and it is sold in Japanese and natural food stores [8][9][8].

Manufacturers add kasu to facial masks, bath powders and face creams, and homemade masks combine it with citrus juice, honey, rice water, aloe vera or rose water [1]. Wikipedia attributes the reported effects mostly to user reports and notes that, because kasu contains alcohol, sunscreen should be applied before a homemade mask [1].

Freeze-dried kasu is described as containing a mixture of triacylglycerols with a tyrosinase-inhibiting extract, one of which, trilinolein, appears in some cosmetics, which is why it is considered a possible anti-browning ingredient [1]. Brewing research has noted that the tyrosinase gene of the koji mold causes browning of sake and sake lees, and that its expression in solid-state culture rises with copper ions [10]. A review of amazake lists skin barrier effects among the functions known from research on sake-lees and koji drinks, with the best-studied effect being on bowel movement, in studies using about 100 mL a day [9].

Rice water is a starch suspension made by draining boiled rice or by boiling rice until it dissolves into the water [2]. Wikipedia reports that it has been used for centuries as a hair treatment by women in China, Japan and Southeast Asia, and that Japanese women in the Heian period (794 to 1185) reportedly kept floor-length hair healthy by bathing it in rice water; the same article describes older use as a food for digestive upset [2].

Fermented rice water is the home preparation in which rice water is left to ferment before use as a hair rinse or toner. On T Nation, a user in 2018 said people were all over fermented rice water for hair loss, ranking it alongside minoxidil and Monistat as things that work [4]. A Hindustan Times headline in 2026 reports that the internet says rice water is effective for hair growth and presents an expert's view on the trending toner [3].

Wikipedia summarises mouse studies suggesting kasu extract may reduce liver fat accumulation, raise branched-chain amino acids in ageing mice, and reduce allergy-like scratching with lactic-fermented kasu, while noting that most health findings come from small or animal studies [1].

A 2025 mouse study found that freeze-dried sake lees and rice koji extract raised collagen accumulation and mineralisation in cultured bone-forming cells and reduced trabecular bone loss in ovariectomised mice, with folic acid and S-adenosylmethionine promoting collagen production in the cells [7]. A 2022 study reported effects of sake lees extract on odontoblast-like cells [6].
No studies found on topical sake lees or fermented rice water for skin or hair appearance.

Related human data on sake lees as a food are a 2025 single-arm trial of eight adults with constipation who consumed 25 or 50 g daily for six weeks; constipation scores improved from 9.2 to 6.8 by week 2, and fecal indole and plasma D-alanine changed [5]. A review of amazake reported that bowel-movement effects have been well studied and that about 100 mL a day had no effect on blood glucose or weight gain in human trials [9].
